questions.q: Print the total of two numbers the user types in, then their difference.

teach.say: + adds, - subtracts and * multiplies. They work on numbers, so cast each input with int() first.

brief: The user types in two whole numbers, one on each line.
Print their total, then the first take away the second.
The difference may be negative.
questions.starter: # Two whole numbers in. Total first, then the difference.

tests.why: 185 instead of 23 means the two lines were joined as text. Cast each one with int() before any arithmetic.
Two equal numbers give a difference of 0, which is a real answer. An empty second line means the subtraction is missing.
5 instead of -5 means you subtracted the other way round. Keep the order the brief gives, even below zero.

questions.fb: The four operators are + - * and / and they work on numbers only, so anything from input() is cast first.

questions.q: Print the cost of some pencils, then half of one price.

teach.say: * multiplies and / divides. In Python / always gives a real number, so the answer keeps a decimal part even when it divides exactly.

brief: The user types in two lines: the price of one pencil in pence, then how many are bought.
Print the total cost of all the pencils.
Then print half the price of one pencil, worked out with / .
questions.starter: # Price in pence, then how many. Total cost, then half a price.

tests.why: 15 instead of 15.0 means the half was worked out another way. / always gives a real number, even when it divides exactly.
A whole number here means // was used. Half of 45 is 22.5, and throwing the .5 away is a different calculation.
A long row of repeated digits on the first line means a string was multiplied: '99' * 2 repeats the text. Cast both with int().

questions.fb: In Python / always gives a real number, which matters when you print it: 15.0 and 15 are not the same output.

questions.q: Print how many full crates the books fill, and the leftovers.

teach.say: // divides and throws the fraction away, so it says how many whole lots fit. % gives what is left over. OCR calls them DIV and MOD.

brief: The user types in two lines: the number of books, then how many one crate holds.
Print how many full crates can be packed.
Then print how many books are left over.
questions.starter: # Books, then crate size. Full crates, then books left over.

tests.why: 7.833 means / was used. A part filled crate is not a full one, so use // , which leaves a whole number.
When the books divide exactly there is nothing left over, so the second answer is 0.
1 instead of 0 means you rounded up. Fewer books than a crate holds fills no crates at all.

questions.fb: // and % are a pair: // says how many whole lots fit, % says what is left behind. Together they lose nothing.

questions.q: Print how many stickers each of 8 pupils gets, and the leftovers.

teach.say: The number you divide by can be a fixed one. // gives the whole lots and % the remainder, so between them nothing is lost.

brief: The user types in one whole number: the total number of stickers.
There are always 8 pupils, so the 8 is fixed in your program, not typed in.
Print how many stickers each pupil gets, then how many are left over.
questions.starter: # Stickers in. Each pupil's share, then the leftovers.

tests.why: 6.25 means / was used for the share. A pupil cannot have a quarter of a sticker, so use // .
They divide exactly here, so nothing is left. An empty second line means the % is missing.
Fewer stickers than pupils means everyone gets 0 and all 5 are left over. A 1 here means the division rounded up.

questions.fb: Splitting a quantity up is always // for the whole lots and % for the remainder, whether it is stickers, pence or pupils in a minibus.

questions.q: Print the area and the volume for a side length the user types in.

teach.say: ** raises a number to a power, so 2 ** 5 is 2 multiplied by itself five times. Do not use ^ , which means something else in Python.

brief: The user types in one whole number: the length of a side.
Print the side to the power 2, the area of the square.
Then print the side to the power 3, the volume of the cube.
questions.starter: # One side length in. Power 2, then power 3.

tests.why: 8 instead of 16 means you multiplied by 2. Squaring 4 means 4 times 4, written 4 ** 2.
21 on the second line means you multiplied by 3. A cube is 7 * 7 * 7, written 7 ** 3.
A side of 1 gives 1 twice, which looks suspicious but is right. One line only means a calculation is missing.

questions.fb: ** is the power operator. Watch out for ^ , which looks like a power in maths but does something else in Python.

questions.q: Print the length of one side of a square, from an area the user types in.

teach.say: The power 0.5 is the square root, and it always gives a real number. Use float() for an input that may have a decimal point.

brief: The user types in the area, which may have a decimal point.
Print only the length of one side.

tests.why: 40.5 means the area was halved rather than rooted. The power 0.5 undoes the power 2.
A crash here means int() was used, and it cannot handle a decimal point. Use float().
10 instead of 10.0 means the answer was cast back to an integer. A fractional power always gives a real number.

questions.fb: Raising to the power 0.5 is the square root, and the answer is a real number even for a perfect square.

questions.q: Round an amount to a whole number, then to 2 decimal places.

teach.say: round(x) rounds to a whole number, and a second number says how many decimal places to keep. An exact half goes to the nearest even number.

brief: The user types in one amount, which may have a decimal point.
Print it rounded to the nearest whole number, using round().
Then print it rounded to 2 decimal places.
questions.starter: # One amount in. Nearest whole number, then 2 decimal places.

tests.why: 4 on the first line is right; 4.0 means the decimals were cut off rather than rounded. int() throws them away, round() looks at them.
This one surprises everybody: an exact half goes to the nearest even whole number, so round(2.5) is 2. Rounding 2.5 to 2 places changes nothing.
3.5 goes up to 4 because 4 is the even neighbour. Compare this with the 2.5 test to see the rule.

questions.fb: round(x) gives a whole number and round(x, 2) keeps two decimal places. Exact halves go to the nearest even value.

questions.q: Print the average of three scores, rounded to 1 decimal place.

teach.say: Dividing often leaves a long string of decimals. round(x, 1) keeps one decimal place and tidies the rest away.

brief: The user types in three whole numbers, one on each line.
Print only their average, rounded to 1 decimal place.
questions.starter: # Three scores in, one rounded average out

tests.why: 5.666666666666667 means the division is right but the round() is missing. 5 means // was used instead of / .
This average is exact, and / still gives a real number, so the answer is 8.0 and not 8.
Add all three before dividing: (a + b + c) / 3. Dividing only the last one gives a much smaller answer.

questions.fb: round() takes a second number for the decimal places to keep, which is how a long division result is made readable.

questions.q: Print two random dice rolls from 1 to 6.

teach.say: random.randint(1, 6) picks a whole number from 1 to 6, and both ends can come up. Seeding first fixes the numbers, so the same seed always gives the same ones.

brief: Start with import random, then random.seed(int(input())). The user types in one whole number, the seed.
Print two random whole numbers from 1 to 6, one on each line.
questions.starter: # Import random, seed it from the input, then roll twice

tests.why: Different numbers from these usually means the wrong ends: randrange(1, 6) stops at 5, and randint(1, 7) can roll a 7.
Two identical numbers mean one roll was stored and printed twice. Two rolls needs two separate calls.
If the first line matches but the second does not, the random module was called an extra time. Every call moves the sequence on.

questions.fb: A seeded random sequence is fixed, which is the only way random code can be marked at all.

questions.q: Print three random numbers from 10 to 20, then their total.

teach.say: Store each random number in a variable as you make it, then add the variables. Calling randint again gives a new number, never the same one back.

brief: Start with import random, then random.seed(int(input())). The user types in one whole number, the seed.
Print three random whole numbers from 10 to 20, one on each line.
Then print their total.
questions.starter: # Import random, seed it from the input, then three numbers and a total

tests.why: If the three numbers are right but the total is not, randint was called again inside the total. That draws a fourth number.
Both ends turn up here. A missing 20 points at randrange(10, 20), which stops at 19; a missing 10 points at randint(11, 20).
A different order from these means something called the random module before your three draws.

questions.fb: Use a variable for every random number you need more than once, because randint never hands the same one back.

questions.q: Print the takings in pence, then in whole pounds and pence.

teach.say: Work the total out once and store it, then use // and % on that variable instead of working it out again.

brief: The user types in two lines: how many rolls were sold, then the price of one in pence.
Print the total takings in pence.
Then print the whole pounds in that total, then the pence left over.
questions.starter: # Rolls and price in. Total pence, whole pounds, pence left over.

tests.why: A long row of repeated digits on the first line means a string was multiplied. Cast both inputs with int().
There are 100 pence in a pound, so // 100 gives the 3 pounds and % 100 gives the 96 pence.
Exactly one pound leaves 0 pence over, and that 0 still has to be printed.

questions.fb: Real programs chain these together: cast the inputs, work out one total, then use // and % to show it in the form asked for.
